answer.sourceLine: Drucker wrote this sentence — word for word — in “Managing for Business Effectiveness,” his article in the May 1963 Harvard Business Review ↗. Quote Investigator ↗ traced it to that article and concluded Drucker should be credited with it. The popular wording is the original, not a later polish.

docMeta.dd: Matches the popular version verbatim, “surely” included

source.excerpt: What is the major problem? It is fundamentally the confusion between effectiveness and efficiency that stands between doing the right things and doing things right. There is surely nothing quite so useless as doing with great efficiency what should not be done at all.
trail: 1907–1908. The joke exists in embryo: a Journal of Education item credits Professor Giddings with defining administration as a systematic way of doing things that need not be done at all, and School Board Journal prints a wit’s line about doing extremely well what should not be done at all — both catalogued by Quote Investigator ↗.

May 1963. Drucker publishes “Managing for Business Effectiveness” in Harvard Business Review ↗, arguing that firms pour resources into problems rather than opportunities. The sentence lands as the close of that argument.

1964, then 1991 and 1995. The rewriting starts almost immediately: a Uniontown, Pennsylvania newspaper filler drops “surely” in November 1964, columnist L. M. Boyd trims it further in 1991, and a 1995 Philadelphia Inquirer column prints a wholly different phrasing under Drucker’s name — the sequence is documented at Quote Investigator ↗.

2017. Quote Investigator publishes its chronology and concludes that Drucker should be credited with the expression he wrote in 1963 ↗, and that Gore Vidal’s 1975 “commercialism” line was probably derived in part from earlier statements.
source.excerptNote: Passage as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from Harvard Business Review’s online archive. HBR’s public page shows only the article’s opening paragraph; the body, including this passage, is paywalled.

author.name: Peter Drucker
author.heading: Who was Peter Drucker?
author.metaLine: 1909–2005 · Austrian-born American management consultant, educator and author
author.bio: Born in Vienna in 1909 and dead in Claremont, California in 2005, Peter Ferdinand Drucker spent six decades arguing that management was a discipline rather than a knack. He taught at Bennington College, then for twenty-one years at New York University, and finally at Claremont Graduate University, where the Drucker Institute counts 39 major books to his name. He is routinely called the founder of modern management — and this sentence is his single most-quoted line about the difference between being busy and being useful.

misattribution.heading: The quote is real — the versions you’ve seen mostly aren’t
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare famous management lines that survives scrutiny: Drucker really wrote it, in the words people use. The trouble is everything that grew around it. Within a year the sentence was already being trimmed, and by the 1990s columnists were quoting rewrites in quotation marks under his name. A separate, similar-sounding line by Gore Vidal gets tangled in as well.

items.scope: “Nothing is less productive than to make more efficient what should not be done at all”
items.who: Credited to Peter Drucker — but not his sentence
items.why: Quote Investigator finds this version in a 1995 Philadelphia Inquirer column, and notes that Inc. republished the same variant in a 2014 productivity listicle. It carries Drucker’s name but shares almost none of his actual wording — see QI’s chronology ↗.

items.scope: “There’s nothing so useless as doing efficiently that which should not be done at all”
items.who: Credited to Peter Drucker — a shortened paraphrase
items.why: Syndicated columnist L. M. Boyd ran this in 1991 with “surely” and “great” both stripped out. QI also documents an even earlier trim: a 1964 filler item in The Evening Standard of Uniontown, Pennsylvania, dropped “surely” barely a year after the original appeared. Both are catalogued by Quote Investigator ↗.

items.scope: “Commercialism is doing well that which should not be done at all”
items.why: A genuinely separate remark, made by Vidal on BBC One in 1975 and printed in The Times Book of Quotations (2000). Vidal openly said he thought he had stolen it from somebody. It is regularly mashed together with Drucker’s sentence online, but the two are not the same quote — QI documents both ↗.

items.scope: “Library efficiency frequently consists of doing very well what need not be done at all”
items.why: The librarian Jesse H. Shera confirmed in writing that this version was his own, according to a 1982 item in American Libraries cited by Quote Investigator ↗. It circulates in library circles and sometimes drifts back onto Drucker.

QI records a 1907 Journal of Education item crediting Professor Giddings with defining administration as a systematic way of doing things that need not be done at all, and a 1908 School Board Journal line about doing extremely well what should not be done at all. These predate Drucker but are jokes about bureaucracy, not the sentence he wrote — read the chronology ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: If you want the line Drucker actually wrote, use this one, with “surely” and “great” intact, and cite “Managing for Business Effectiveness,” Harvard Business Review, May 1963 ↗.

context.heading: Why this sentence stuck
lead: The line is not a standalone aphorism — it is the punchline of a diagnosis. In the same passage Drucker complains that in every allocation of business resources he had ever examined, the bulk of time, work, attention and money went to problems rather than opportunities, and to areas where even extraordinary performance would barely move results. The fix, he argued, was to stop confusing effectiveness with efficiency.

That framing is what gave the sentence legs. Efficiency measures how well you do the thing; effectiveness asks whether the thing is worth doing. Drucker’s formulation makes the first worthless without the second, in one breath, which is why it has been recycled by consultants, librarians and productivity bloggers for six decades — usually in a slightly worse rewrite.
detailsBody: The underlying gag is older than Drucker. Quote Investigator records a 1907 item in The Journal of Education in which Professor Giddings is credited with defining “administration” as a systematic way of doing things that need not be done at all, and a 1908 line in School Board Journal attributed to an unnamed wit: doing extremely well what should not be done at all.

What Drucker added was the business frame. The earlier versions are jabs at bureaucrats; his is a claim about where a company’s scarce resources actually go, embedded in an argument about opportunity versus problem-solving. That is why his phrasing, not the 1907 one, is the version people quote.
context.pull: The confusion between effectiveness and efficiency stands between doing the right things and doing things right.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes Peter Drucker should be credited with this expression, which he wrote in the May 1963 Harvard Business Review article “Managing for Business Effectiveness”; QI transcribes the passage containing the exact sentence, including the word “surely.”

Quote Investigator documents the precursors and variants: a 1907 Journal of Education item crediting Professor Giddings; a 1908 School Board Journal line; a November 1964 Uniontown, Pennsylvania Evening Standard filler that drops “surely”; L. M. Boyd’s 1991 trimmed version; a 1995 Philadelphia Inquirer variant later reused by Inc. in 2014; Jesse H. Shera’s library version reported in American Libraries (1982); and Gore Vidal’s 1975 BBC One “commercialism” remark, printed in The Times Book of Quotations (2000).

Harvard Business Review’s archive lists “Managing for Business Effectiveness” by Peter F. Drucker, From the Magazine (May 1963), with only the opening paragraph shown publicly and PDF/reprint purchase offered; the page carries a Harvard Business School Publishing copyright notice.

Quote Investigator’s companion article examines Drucker’s related formula “Efficiency is doing things right; effectiveness is doing the right things,” noting Drucker presented the concept multiple times and that the phrasing evolved over time.
Wikiquote’s Peter Drucker page organises his quotations by book and decade; it does not contain this sentence, and its Misattributed section lists only “Culture eats strategy for breakfast.”

The Drucker Institute states Drucker was born 19 November 1909 in Vienna, Austria and died 11 November 2005; that he taught at Bennington College, at New York University for 21 years, and at Claremont Graduate University; and that he published 39 major books.

Wikipedia gives Peter Ferdinand Drucker’s dates as 19 November 1909 (Vienna) to 11 November 2005 (Claremont, California), describes him as a management consultant, educator and author, and lists Managing for Results (New York: Harper & Row, 1964) in his bibliography.
